title: Writing: The Most Underrated Twenty-First Century Skill
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that writing is the most underrated skill for students to leave school with, and that schools underinvest in it. He grants the economic case for writing but insists that school is not a widget factory, and that writing also makes people better readers, thinkers, speakers and listeners. He cites the Nation's Report Card, under which only about a quarter of students write proficiently, and he defines proficiency modestly as writing that accomplishes its communicative purpose. His proposed remedy follows David Conley: increase both the quantity and the quality of writing students are asked to produce. He ends by calling this fruit so low-hanging that it is practically underground.
points: Writing is both an economic gatekeeper skill and a broader human good that sharpens reading, thinking, speaking and listening.
NAEP data show only about a quarter of students write proficiently, which makes capable writers rare and advantaged.
Proficiency is defined modestly as writing that accomplishes its communicative purpose, such as an email someone can understand without difficulty.
Following Conley, the fix is two steps: more writing, and better writing, expected from students.
Stuart rejects a purely workforce framing of schooling while still making the economic case, so the argument holds on both grounds.
quotes: I struggle to imagine putting together a solid argument for why we wouldn't want all of our students to be capable writers when they graduate. Writing well is an obvious good.

And of course, just as school should not be conceived of as a place that produces widgets prepared to enter the economy, writing is not only about dollars and cents. A proficient writer is able to journal through mental health struggles, articulate complex thoughts, and communicate in a measured manner.
Writing makes us better readers, better thinkers, better speakers, and better listeners. Through writing, we can inform, explain, argue, entertain, and inspire.

Unfortunately, those who graduate today with the ability to write have one more huge advantage: they're rare. According to the most recent (as of this writing) Nation's Report Card on Writing, only about a quarter of kids and graduates are able to write proficiently.

We're not talking about the ability to mimic Shakespeare here — proficient writing is the ability to compose an email that someone can read and understand without difficulty. As NAEP says in their report, this is the ability to accomplish one's communicative purpose in writing. When you're proficient, your writing does what it was supposed to do.
